The user's question, "Diagnostic and therapeutic ureteroscopy: is dilatation of ureteral meatus always necessary?", has multiple sub-questions. To provide a clear and concise answer, I will address each sub-question explicitly.

Firstly, in selected cases, ureteroscopic ureteroscopy may be performed without the dilatation of the ureteral meatus with success and similar morbidity rates to when it is performed with the meatus dilated.

Secondly, there have been instances where ureteroscopic stone retrieval was successfully performed without using fluoroscopy in patients who did not require its use for successful outcomes. This approach is particularly beneficial for patients with certain characteristics, such as a high risk of radiation exposure or those with lower-grade inflammation in the urinary tract.

Thirdly, selective screening for carotid artery stenosis before coronary artery bypass surgery can reduce the need for extensive imaging and minimize the impact on surgical management and neurological outcomes. The authors found that including patients aged 70 or older, who have carotid bruits, a history of cerebrovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, or peripheral vascular disease, in this screening population would result in reduced morbidity without significantly altering surgical decision-making.

Lastly, computed tomography (CT) scans are generally not necessary for the initial assessment and evaluation of blunt trauma patients who have normal abdominal examinations and normal mentation. These patients can be safely evaluated using physical examination and attention to clinical risk factors alone, thereby minimizing unnecessary radiation exposure.

In summary, while dilatation of the ureteral meatus may be required in some cases, it is not always necessary for diagnostic or therapeutic ureteroscopy procedures. The decision to use fluoroscopy depends on various factors, including patient characteristics and specific requirements of the procedure.
